opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to a few things, and honestly most people underestimate how many of them have to be good at the same time.

The first is physics fidelity, especially contact. Rigid-body dynamics for a robot arm moving through free space is mostly solved. What's not solved is what happens when the gripper touches something: friction, deformation, slip, soft materials, cables, cloth, liquids. That's where almost all the interesting manipulation happens, and it's where simulators still diverge from reality. If your contact model is wrong, the policy you train learns to exploit artifacts of the simulator, not the real world.

The second is the gap between "looks right" and "is right." A lot of progress in rendering has made simulation visually convincing, which matters for vision-based policies. But visual realism without physical realism gives you false confidence. You need both, and you need them consistent with each other, so the object that looks heavy actually behaves heavy.

Third is scale and diversity of content. A simulator is only as useful as the worlds you can put in it. If you have ten kitchens and fifty objects, your robot learns ten kitchens and fifty objects. To generalize you need huge numbers of assets with correct geometry, materials, articulation, and mass properties, and today building those is still very labor-intensive. Generating them automatically, including from real-world scans or with generative models, is a big part of the answer.

Fourth, and maybe most important, is a tight loop with reality. Simulation shouldn't be a replacement for real data; it should be calibrated by it. You collect real-world data, measure where sim and reality disagree, fix the model or randomize over the uncertainty, and repeat. The teams that make progress treat sim-to-real as an engineering discipline with metrics, not as a one-time leap of faith.

And finally, speed and accessibility. If it's accurate but takes a week to run an experiment, or only a few experts can set it up, it won't move the industry. It has to be fast enough to generate the massive amounts of experience that learning methods need, and open enough that researchers and companies can build on a shared foundation.

So my short answer is: accurate contact physics, consistent sensing, massive and realistic content, continuous calibration against the real world, and enough speed and openness that everyone can actually use it. When those come together, simulation stops being a toy and becomes the place where most robot learning happens.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts visually convincing simulation with missing physical realism and explains that incorrect contact behavior makes interaction-trained policies exploit simulator artifacts.

r002.rationale: It mentions articulation among asset properties, but does not say that an object's ability to articulate fails to establish accurate dynamics.

r003.rationale: It calls for many diverse assets to support generalization, but does not clearly identify coverage of the real-world distribution of object variants as the requirement.

r004.rationale: The response discusses simulation and reality disagreeing, especially in contact physics, but does not identify simulated robot capabilities as substantially misrepresenting the real robot's capabilities.

r005.rationale: It mentions consistent sensing and simulation speed, but does not identify perception in the loop as a bottleneck to parallel execution of reinforcement-learning environments.

r006.rationale: It describes repeatedly calibrating simulation against real-world data, but does not specify testing simulation-trained algorithms on real robots to evaluate their performance.

r007.rationale: It lists accuracy and content scale as separate needs, but does not clearly argue that producing more simulation cannot compensate for insufficient simulation quality.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that "good enough" simulation isn't really one thing, it's three things that have to come together, and most of the industry has only been serious about one of them.

The first is physics fidelity, and that's the one everyone talks about. Rigid body contact is largely solved for things like locomotion. You can train a quadruped or a humanoid to walk in simulation and transfer it to hardware with a modest amount of domain randomization. But the moment you move to manipulation, you hit the long tail: deformables, cloth, liquids, cables, friction that changes when a surface gets a little greasy. Those are still hard, and the gap there is not a matter of more GPUs. It's a matter of better contact models and, frankly, better validation against real measurements. A lot of simulators look plausible and are quantitatively wrong.

The second piece is sensor realism, especially vision. For years sim was good at dynamics and bad at pixels. That's changed quickly with photorealistic rendering, neural reconstruction, and generative models. Now you can build a scene from a few phone videos and get rendering that's close enough that a visuomotor policy doesn't immediately notice the difference. I'd argue that's where the biggest recent leap has been, because it lets simulation feed the same kind of large vision-language-action models that are driving the rest of the field.

The third piece is the one I think is actually the bottleneck now, and it's not technical glamour at all: content and scale. A simulator with perfect physics and perfect rendering is useless if you have fifty hand-built scenes. What advances the industry is millions of diverse, task-relevant, semantically meaningful environments, with objects that have correct mass, articulation, and affordances, plus a pipeline that generates tasks and success criteria automatically. That's a data engineering and tooling problem. It's the unglamorous layer, and whoever solves it well will matter more than whoever shaves a few percent off a contact solver's error.

And then I'd add a mindset shift. Simulation shouldn't be judged on whether it perfectly replicates reality. It should be judged on whether policies trained in it transfer, and whether it lets you evaluate a robot thousands of times before you ever risk the hardware. The goal is a closed loop: real data calibrates the sim, the sim generates orders of magnitude more experience, and the real world remains the final exam. When teams treat sim as the training ground and evaluation harness rather than a substitute for reality, that's when it actually moves the industry forward.

r002.rationale: It mentions articulation and physical inaccuracies separately, but does not explain that an object's ability to articulate does not establish accurate dynamics.

r003.rationale: It calls for millions of diverse, task-relevant environments, but does not identify coverage of real-world object variants as a requirement.

r004.rationale: It discusses transfer from simulation to hardware, but does not identify that a simulated robot's physical capabilities can substantially misrepresent its real counterpart.

r006.rationale: It describes a closed loop in which real data calibrates simulation, policies trained in simulation are judged by transfer, and the real world serves as the final evaluation.

r007.rationale: It says simulation needs both fidelity and scale, but does not clearly argue that producing large quantities of simulation cannot substitute for sufficient simulation quality.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to ask: good enough for what? A simulator can look very realistic and still get the physics wrong in ways that matter to a robot. If you’re training a robot to pick up an object, friction, contact, and the behavior of the sensors may matter much more than how beautiful the scene looks.

So I would start with a real task and measure whether improvements in simulation lead to improvements on the physical robot. That gives you a feedback loop: run experiments, identify where the simulator disagrees with reality, and improve the parts that affect performance. You also need to represent uncertainty, because no single model will capture every surface, object, or operating condition.

Then there’s the practical side. Simulation has to be fast, reliable, and easy enough for engineers to use every day. Can they reproduce a failure? Can they test a software change across thousands of scenarios? Can they trust the results enough to decide what to test on hardware next?

To me, the goal isn’t a perfect virtual world. It’s a tool that measurably reduces the time and cost of building robots that work in the real world.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss object articulation or explain why articulation would not establish accurate dynamics.

r003.rationale: It mentions that models cannot capture every object and operating condition, but does not call for covering the real-world distribution of object variants.

r004.rationale: It does not compare a simulated robot’s physical capabilities with those of its real-world counterpart.

r005.rationale: It mentions sensor behavior, but not perception as a bottleneck to running reinforcement-learning simulation environments in parallel.

r006.rationale: It calls for measuring whether simulation improvements improve performance on physical robots and describes iterating by finding and correcting discrepancies with reality.

r007.rationale: It emphasizes simulation quality and testing many scenarios, but does not argue that producing large quantities of simulation cannot replace sufficient quality.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to define “good enough” by what transfers to the real robot. A simulation can look very realistic and still get the things that matter wrong—contact, friction, sensor noise, or timing. So the first question is: what decision are we using this simulation to make?

If we’re training a robot to manipulate objects, we need to capture the variation it will encounter, rather than assume one perfectly modeled environment. And we need a tight loop with real-world experiments: run the policy, see where it fails, and use those failures to improve the simulator.

For the industry, usability matters too. If every team needs months of specialist work to build a scene and calibrate a robot, adoption will be limited. We need tools that make it easy to create environments, run experiments at scale, and measure whether improvements in simulation actually produce improvements on hardware.

So I would focus on three things: the right physics for the task, a continuous feedback loop with real robots, and a workflow that engineers can use every day. The real benchmark is whether simulation reduces the time and cost of getting a reliable robot into the world.
